Expert Report: All About the Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Meir Kahane – A Multi-Layered Analysis of Ideology and Activism
This expert report provides a comprehensive analysis of Rabbi Meir Kahane’s life, detailing his transition from mainstream religious roles to the leadership of radical movements that fused theological redemption with political violence. The text is structured to examine his biography, the ideological foundations of "The Jewish Idea," and the subsequent legal and rabbinic repercussions of his militant Kahanist doctrine. Central to his worldview was a reinterpretation of traditional concepts, where he viewed the presence of non-Jews in Israel as a desecration of God’s name and rejected liberal ethics as a psychological weakness. Ultimately, the document highlights how his activities forced the Israeli legal system to adopt defensive democratic measures and led to his organizations being internationally designated as terrorist entities.
Expert Report: All About the Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Meir Kahane – A Multi-Layered Analysis of Ideology and Activism
Introduction: Rabbi Meir Kahane and Kahanism as a Theological-Political Ideology
Rabbi Meir David Kahane (1932–1990) was a central and revolutionary figure in Israeli and Jewish politics in the second half of the 20th century. Kahane, who was a rabbi, a politician, a leader of the extreme right and head of the "Jewish Idea" yeshiva [1, 2], was assassinated by an Arab-Muslim assassin in Manhattan in 1990.[1] Kahane's work was characterized by a unique synthesis of forceful activism and political violence, rooted in a radical interpretation of the Jewish theology of chosenness and redemption.
This report is intended to provide a comprehensive analysis of Kahane's Torah teaching and political work. It will examine the biographical background that led him from the accepted religious-Zionist frameworks to the development of Kahanism, the theological foundations of "the Jewish Idea" as a messianic-activist doctrine, and its legal and political consequences for the boundaries of Israeli democracy and for rabbinic discourse.
Part One: From National-Religious Education to Extreme Activism (His Organizational Work)
Chapter 1: The Biographical Path and the Radical Growth (1932–1974)
Rabbi Kahane began his path within the accepted Zionist and religious establishment both in the United States and in Israel. In his youth he was active in the Betar movement between 1946 and 1951, and later was active within the framework of the Bnei Akiva movement between 1952 and 1954.[3] After his Torah studies he served as a community rabbi in Queens, New York, in the Howard Beach congregation between 1958 and 1960.[3] Parallel to his tenure as a rabbi, Kahane developed a journalistic career lasting many years: he served as editor of the Jewish weekly "The Jewish Press" from 1962 to 1969, and was a regular columnist in this newspaper from 1961 until the day of his death in 1990.[3]
The biographical data testify to Kahane's strategic existence on two parallel planes: he conducted a legitimate and highly influential career in the established press for three decades [3], and at the same time founded and led radical movements. The Jewish Defense League (JDL), which he founded in the United States in 1968 [3], was his forceful response to what he perceived as the failure of the Jewish leadership in the Diaspora to deal with antisemitism and assimilation by means of negotiation or passivity. Later, in 1974, after he immigrated to Israel, Kahane founded the "Kach" movement.[3] The long-standing connection with a legitimate journalistic platform, alongside his allegedly paramilitary activity, enabled Kahane to leverage his influence and to establish a rhetorical infrastructure for spreading his extreme ideology, even while he was involved in controversial actions. His transition from the moderate religious Zionism of Bnei Akiva and Betar to the violent activism of the JDL and "Kach" reflects a deep distrust in the ability of the existing frameworks to protect Jewish interests without the use of vigorous force.
Chapter 2: Political Kahanism and the Imperative of Violence (1974–1990)
Kahane was elected to the 11th Knesset in 1984 as the sole representative of the "Kach" movement.[2] His political activity in the Knesset was chiefly a platform for spreading his extreme ideas and for developing a political doctrine that justified the use of violence and the denial of democracy toward his opponents. Kahanist rhetoric was characterized by ideological radicalization and by an absolute rejection of compromise. Kahane argued that "every concession will give birth to world pressure for more concessions" [1], and thereby disqualified in advance any attempt by the Israeli government to reach peace agreements or territorial compromise. In his view, if "peace is truly beautiful, it must not be bought at the price of freedom."[1]
Kahane clearly defined his internal and external enemy. He claimed that the people of the left were in essence traitors or perverted, and that "in their hearts, the leftists do not believe that we have a right to live in Israel."[1] He even claimed that he understands the Arabs and vice versa, and that "none of us understands the leftists."[1] This use of polarizing language was intended to undermine the legitimacy of anyone who did not share his conception, including the Israeli media, which he called "the PLO's most powerful weapon."[1]
Kahane's doctrine was based on the need to replace the liberal feelings of guilt with the concept of greatness.[1] He defined Jewish guilt feelings as "a special and specific kind of Jewish AIDS."[1] By formulating guilt as a "disease" to be cured, Kahane provided a religious and psychological justification for rejecting liberal and universal ethics. This approach enabled him to position his uncompromising demands as the only authentic Jewish way, and thereby made Kahanism an ideology immune to traditional moral or political criticism.

The table demonstrates the transnational and violent character of the movements Kahane founded, these organizations having been classified as terrorist organizations by law-enforcement authorities on two different continents.[4, 5] This fact emphasizes that political violence was not merely a tactical tool for Kahane, but an essential component of his doctrine for achieving ideological goals.
Part Two: His Torah Teaching: The Foundations of "the Jewish Idea"
Chapter 3: The Kahanist Doctrine of Redemption: The Revolution of Theological Activism
The theological basis of Kahane's teaching – "the original Jewish idea" – drew concepts from existing streams in religious Zionism, but radicalized them into a binding doctrinaire system. Kahane accepted Rav Kook's conception that the establishment of the State of Israel constitutes "the beginning of the flowering of our redemption" [9], and he even used to recite the prayer for the welfare of the State.[9] Nevertheless, Kahane firmly rejected messianic passivity, which he saw as an evasion of religious responsibility. Instead of passively waiting for a miracle or a messianic revelation, Kahane demanded "activism and partnership in the Zionist process."[9]
Redemption, according to Kahane, is not a by-product of inner tranquility or international agreement, but stems from confrontation with and resistance to the gentiles.[9] He explained the need for an independent and Jewish State of Israel by means of the theological argument that the life of the people of Israel in exile, under gentile rule, constitutes a "desecration of God's name" (chillul Hashem).[9] In this way Kahane transferred the concept of chillul Hashem, which traditionally concerns the ethical and moral conduct of the individual toward God and toward human beings, to the territorial and geopolitical plane.
This theological innovation is the key to understanding Kahanism: if chillul Hashem is defined by gentile rule or gentile presence in the Land of Israel, then the central religious commandment is territorial purification and the establishment of absolute Jewish rule. This conception creates a direct and binding link between messianic theology and the radical political demand for the expulsion of the Arabs, and gives the national struggle the status of a holy war that is an inseparable part of the process of redemption.[9]
Chapter 4: Solving "the Arab Problem": The Purification of the Land as a Religious Imperative
Kahane's teaching based its attitude to the Arabs on the conception of the chosenness of the Jewish people as a superior people, which is obliged to "separate from the nations and from their culture."[9] From the principle of chosenness and superiority it was derived that the presence of gentiles in the Land of Israel is a desecration of God's name, and therefore "the solution of the problem of the Arabs in the Land is of central importance, since its solution will purify the Land of the desecration of God's name involved in their presence in it."[9]
Within the framework of the doctrinaire analysis, Kahane carried out a systematic reduction of the political and national conflict to an absolute theological conflict. Since separation is a divine command, any kind of partnership or coexistence was perceived as theologically impossible, since it violates the principle of separation and perpetuates the desecration of God's name.[9] The rejection of compromises and the demand for expulsion are therefore not merely extreme political preferences, but religious commands imposed on the chosen people. At first Kahane argued that the emigration of the Arabs should be encouraged "voluntarily only" [9], but the logical course of his teaching led necessarily to the conclusion that forced expulsion is required in order to ensure the purification of the Land and the completion of the redemption.

Part Three: The Consequences, the Disqualification and the Theological-Legal Legacy
Chapter 5: Kahanism and Democracy: The Legal and Legislative Confrontation
The influence of Kahane's work on the Israeli legal system was dramatic. Kahane and his movement are considered the formative factor that led to the establishment of mechanisms of "defensive democracy" in Israel. Following Kahane's entry into the Knesset, the Knesset approved in 1985 the amendment to Basic Law: The Knesset, which added section 7A.[8] This section provides that a list or a candidate whose "goals or actions" include "the negation of the existence of the State of Israel as the state of the Jewish people" or explicit racism shall not participate in elections.[8]
Kahanism thus served as a borderline test case for Israeli constitutional law, since it compelled the system to deal with the paradox of democratic tolerance toward anti-democratic movements. The legal analysis emphasizes that section 7A is an exception to the fundamental right to vote and to be elected, which is at the core of the democratic system.[6] Therefore, the interpretation of this section requires that it be narrowed as far as possible, and its use is justified only when there is a grave danger to the existence and security of the state or to its democratic regime.[6] The need for such legislation stems directly from the conception that the Kahanist ideology, which advocated expulsion on an ethnic-religious basis [9] and the denial of citizenship to certain bodies, constituted an existential threat to the constitutional character of the state, since it operated by using democracy against itself.
Chapter 6: International Status and the Organizational Legacy
Rabbi Kahane was assassinated in New York in November 1990.[1] His death did not end the existence of the Kahanist ideology, and its influence continued through the organizations he had founded. The Jewish Defense League (JDL) served as an active terrorist organization during the first two decades of its existence, and it was even classified as such by the FBI in the report "Terrorism 2000/2001."[4, 5] The JDL was suspected of involvement in attacks, including the bombing of the offices of Sol Hurok in Manhattan in 1972, in which one employee was killed.[5]
The parallel designation of Kahanist movements as terrorist organizations on two continents – the JDL in the United States and "Kach" and "Kahane Chai" in Israel (declared terrorist organizations in 1994) [7] – places Kahanism as a transnational ideology that uses religious justification for political violence. Kahane himself published the foundations of his Torah teaching in books such as Or ha-Ra'ayon ("The Light of the Idea") and Perush ha-Makabi – Devarim ("The Maccabee Commentary – Deuteronomy") [2], which constitute the theological basis for justifying violent activism. The continued existence of these groups after Kahane's assassination shows that the ideology he founded, which combines a belief in Jewish supremacy with the imperative to use force, implanted violent patterns of action as a legitimate mode of action.
Chapter 7: Torah Criticism and Rabbinic Delegitimization
Rabbi Kahane's extreme teaching aroused sharp opposition not only in the political and legal system, but also within the rabbinic establishment itself, both Haredi and religious-Zionist. The opposition was not merely political, but touched on the theological essence and on the question of the halakhic authority empowered to interpret Zionism and redemption.
The rabbinic establishment, which seeks to preserve a balanced and ethical image of Judaism, saw Kahanism as a real threat. Attempts to thwart the appointment of Kahanist candidates to senior rabbinic posts were made by means of confidential campaigns, on the claim that supporting them harms "the honor of the Chief Rabbinate of Israel."[10] This fierce opposition from within testifies that the establishment rabbis feared that the Kahanist approach, which sanctifies ethnic supremacy and permits extreme violence, might be interpreted as the accepted halakhic outlook, and thereby undermine the moral and ethical legitimacy of the moderate rabbinate.[10] This is a struggle over defining the boundaries of halakha and morality in the period of political redemption, in which the establishment sought to restore the principles of traditional Jewish ethics that limit the use of force in the face of political-religious extremism.
Summary and Analytical Conclusions
Rabbi Meir Kahane founded an ideological movement, Kahanism, which constitutes a unique synthesis of religious political activism and the radicalization of fundamental Torah concepts. The analysis shows that Kahanism is not an accidental political deviation, but a cohesive doctrinaire system that influenced the Israeli sphere on several central planes.
1. Theological transformation: Kahane carried out a theological revolution by turning spiritual concepts (such as chillul Hashem) into binding territorial and political mandates. By defining the Arab presence in the Land of Israel as a desecration of God's name, he provided absolute religious legitimacy for the demand for expulsion.[9] Setting "the Jewish AIDS" (guilt feelings) against the idea of greatness [1] was intended to create an ideological immunity that prevents external moral criticism.
2. Legal consequences and democratic defense: Kahanism proved itself an existential threat to the liberal and democratic character of the State of Israel. His movement compelled the legal system to create constitutional mechanisms of self-defense (section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset) [8], and thereby redefined the boundaries of freedom of expression and of political participation in the state.
3. Essential violence: The designation of his organizations, the JDL and "Kach," as terrorist organizations by American and Israeli authorities [4, 5] establishes that the use of violence is an inherent and ideologically justified component of the Kahanist doctrine, and not the preserve of a handful of extremists.
Despite his being pushed out of the political system (by means of disqualification) and out of the rabbinic establishment (by means of delegitimization) [10], Kahanism continues to serve as an ideological infrastructure for extreme streams on the Israeli right, and represents the theological-political extreme line of religious Zionism. Dealing with his legacy requires a multi-layered understanding of the way in which Torah ideas can be converted into violent political mandates.
